planting.note: Plant container stock in spring into well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Lama is extremely slow-growing, taking 5-10 years or more to mature into a garden-scale tree.

directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained soil; Lama is an endemic Hawaiian ebony-family tree reaching 20-40 feet, found naturally in dry and mesic forest understory across the islands. It is extremely slow-growing, often taking a decade or more to reach a garden-scale size, so patience is essential. Tiny flowers give way to small orange, persimmon-family fruit, and the tree holds cultural significance in traditional Hawaiian practice, often used in hula platform construction.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring into well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Alahe'e tolerates both dry and wet sites once established, a flexible native tree for Hawaiian landscaping.

directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained soil; Alahe'e is an indigenous shrub to small tree, ranging from 6 feet in dwarfed dry-site forms up to 30 feet in better conditions, bearing fragrant clustered white flowers resembling mock orange that bloom intermittently through the year, followed by small black fruit. It is a signature species of leeward dry forest reserves like Waikoloa and tolerates both dry and wetter sites once established, making it a versatile choice for Hawaiian native landscaping.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring into well-drained soil in full sun; Koai'a is the dry-forest sister species of koa, actively propagated for restoration and landscaping despite wild-population concern.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; Koai'a is the dry-forest sister species of the better-known koa (Acacia koa), with denser wood, a shorter stature to about 30 feet, gray-green sickle-shaped phyllodes, and pale puffball flowers. It is restricted naturally to leeward dry forest below roughly 3,000 feet and is listed as a federal species of concern in the wild, but it is actively propagated by Hawaii's state forestry nursery and specialty native-plant nurseries for restoration and landscape use. Drought-tolerant once established.
sources: Hawaii Division of Forestry and Wildlife nursery

subcategory: native Hawaiian dry forest groundcover shrub

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring into well-drained soil in full sun; 'Akia is described as the most commonly used native groundcover in Hawaiian landscaping.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; 'Akia is a prostrate to sprawling shrub reaching 2-4 feet tall and spreading to 10 feet, bearing small yellow-green tubular flowers nearly year-round and crimson berries. It shows exceptional tolerance of salt spray, wind, heat, and drought, making it a specialist for leeward and dry coastal Hawaiian landscaping, and is described as the most commonly used native groundcover in the islands. It tolerates partial shade but performs best and spreads most densely in full sun.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring into well-drained soil in full sun; Pa'u o Hi'iaka blooms nearly year-round, a reliable groundcover for dry Hawaiian coastal and lowland sites.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; Pa'u o Hi'iaka is a prostrate, mat-forming native Hawaiian morning-glory relative, bearing funnel-shaped lavender-to-white flowers about an inch wide that open nearly year-round. It is a natural strand and dry-coastal groundcover across the main islands, very drought- and salt-tolerant once established, and named in Hawaiian legend for the goddess Hi'iaka's skirt. It spreads to form a dense, low mat, useful for stabilizing dry, sunny slopes.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring into well-drained soil in full sun; Kulu'i is grown chiefly for its silvery foliage, a distinctive textural accent in a dry Hawaiian native planting.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; Kulu'i is a silvery-haired native Hawaiian shrub to small tree, ranging from about 3 feet in exposed dwarf forms to 30 feet in favorable conditions, grown chiefly for its fuzzy, pale silver-green foliage that provides a striking textural contrast in a dry native planting. Inconspicuous flowers appear in small spikes. It is characteristic of open dry forest, exposed ridges, and lava fields from sea level to about 3,000 feet, and needs minimal water once established.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring into well-drained soil in full sun; 'Ohe Makai is deciduous, unusual among Hawaiian native trees, dropping its leaves during summer dry-season dormancy.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; 'Ohe Makai is a small to medium native Hawaiian tree and one of the few native Hawaiian species that is deciduous, dropping its leaves during the summer dry season rather than holding foliage year-round like most of the island flora. It grows in dry and occasionally mesic forest and is becoming uncommon in the wild, though it is actively cultivated in restoration plantings and specialty native-plant landscaping. Its deciduous habit is a genuine botanical curiosity worth noting when siting it in a garden.
sources: Future Forests / Hui Ku Maoli Ola nursery network

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring into well-drained soil in full sun; handle 'Akoko with care, since like other Euphorbia species its sap is an irritant.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; 'Akoko is a highly variable native Hawaiian spurge, ranging from prostrate 2-foot groundcover mats to erect 6-foot shrubs with thick, glabrous leaves, found in dry and lowland forest and dry coastal sites such as Ka'ena Point and the Wai'anae range. Inconspicuous cyathia-type flowers are typical of the genus. Handle it with care, since like other Euphorbia species the milky sap is an irritant to skin and eyes. Drought-tolerant once established, needing minimal irrigation beyond the first growing season.
